reasoning_summary: The statement is a definitional-inclusion result: a real semi-inner product space is a complex semi-inner product space. The proof is a three-item citation (the two definitions plus the lemma 'Real Semi-Inner Product is Complex Semi-Inner Product'), which is exactly the content needed: once the semi-inner product itself is known to satisfy the complex axioms, the space-level statement is immediate from unfolding the two space definitions. I attempted a concrete counterexample and failed. Candidate: V = R with <x,y> = xy, and the degenerate candidate V = R^2 with <(x1,x2),(y1,y2)> = x1*y1 (semi-definite, kernel spanned by (0,1)). Check the complex axioms with the field embedded via R subset C: conjugate symmetry holds because conj(<y,x>) = <y,x> = <x,y> for real values (e.g. <(1,5),(1,-3)> = 1 = conj(<(1,-3),(1,5)>)); (sesqui)linearity in the appropriate argument holds for every scalar available in the space, since conjugation is the identity on R so the conjugate-linearity condition <x, lambda*y> = conj(lambda)<x,y> collapses to the real-linearity condition <x, lambda*y> = lambda<x,y>; and nonnegativity <x,x> = x1^2 >= 0 holds, with the Cauchy-Schwarz/semi-definiteness bound |<x,y>|^2 = (x1 y1)^2 = <x,x><y,y> satisfied with equality. Every axiom of the complex notion is therefore inherited, so no real semi-inner product space fails to be a complex one under the shared subfield-of-C formulation the two definitions use. The only way to break the claim would be to read 'complex semi-inner product space' as requiring the underlying space to be a genuine C-vector space (so that multiplication by i must be defined, which fails for V = R); but that reading would falsify the theorem statement itself, not any inference the proof makes, and the cited definitions on which the proof rests are the ones stated over a subfield of C. Nothing the proof actually asserts is refutable, so I report VALID.
